earth-formation.summary: Accretion of the Earth from the solar nebula, dated by radiometric analysis of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial minerals.
earth-formation.significance: Everything else on this timeline is compressed into the last tenth of it. If the Earth's history were a single day, recorded human history would occupy the final second.

first-oceans.summary: As the surface cooled below the boiling point, the steam atmosphere condensed and fell, and the planet acquired the oceans it has had almost ever since — the first surface on Earth that could hold chemistry together long enough for anything to start.
first-oceans.significance: Liquid water arrived within a few hundred million years of the planet itself, and has never entirely left. Everything else on this timeline happens in it or beside it.
first-oceans.note: The early bracket rests on zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, whose oxygen isotope ratios are read as contact with liquid water at 4.4 Ga - a reading that is disputed. The late bracket is firmer: pillow basalts and water-laid sediments in Greenland put oceans beyond doubt by 3.8 Ga. The popular image of rain falling for thousands of years without stopping is inference rather than evidence; how long condensation took, and whether it happened once or repeatedly as impacts boiled it off again, is not settled.

sources.title: Nature — Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago

origin-of-life.summary: Self-replicating chemistry appeared within a few hundred million years of the Earth becoming habitable — startlingly fast, which is one reason the question of life elsewhere stays open.
origin-of-life.significance: Life appeared almost as soon as the planet could support it. That speed is the main reason biologists take the possibility of life elsewhere seriously.
origin-of-life.note: Carbon isotope signatures in Greenland zircons hint at 4.1 Ga; undisputed microfossils are closer to 3.5 Ga. How life began remains unsolved.

great-oxidation.summary: Cyanobacteria filled the atmosphere with oxygen, poisoning most existing life and rusting the oceans. The largest pollution event in history, and the reason anything breathes today.
great-oxidation.significance: The first mass extinction was caused by a lifeform poisoning its own atmosphere. It is also the reason anything can breathe.

eukaryotes.summary: One cell engulfed another and kept it, producing the mitochondrion. Every plant, animal and fungus descends from that single merger.
eukaryotes.note: Wikidata gives 2.7 Ga, a figure resting on sterane biomarkers from Australian shales that later work attributes to contamination. The bracket here follows the fossil and molecular evidence instead, where Grypania at about 2.1 Ga is the earliest widely accepted candidate.

image.credit: Daniel Vaulot, CNRS, Station Biologique de Roscoff

multicellular-life.summary: Cells began staying together and specialising, producing the soft frond-like Ediacaran organisms that preceded the Cambrian and mostly left no descendants.

snowball-earth.summary: Ice reached the tropics twice in the Cryogenian, for spans of millions of years, and the Earth escaped only because volcanic carbon dioxide kept accumulating in an atmosphere with no rain to wash it out — ending in a greenhouse as violent as the freeze.
snowball-earth.significance: The planet has a second stable state, and it has been in it. Ice reflects sunlight, which makes more ice, which reflects more sunlight - and the way out was not sunlight but volcanoes, over millions of years.
snowball-earth.note: Two glaciations, not one - the Sturtian from about 717 to 660 Ma and the Marinoan from about 650 to 635 Ma. How complete the ice was is the live argument: a hard snowball frozen to the equator, or a slushball with open water in the tropics that kept photosynthesis going. Glacial deposits at sea level in the tropics are the evidence either way.
